# The Reality War

## Interpretations of "The Reality War"

The phrase "The Reality War" serves as the title for multiple distinct works and concepts, each with a different scope and level of documented notability. An encyclopedic examination reveals three primary interpretations: a science fiction novel series, a television episode from the long-running British science fiction program *Doctor Who*, and an unattested rhetorical framing used in discourse about information warfare. The most prominent and extensively documented of these is the television episode, which forms the central focus of this report due to its significant cultural resonance and the wealth of available source material detailing its production, plot, and reception. The other interpretations, while verifiable, lack the same degree of widespread attention and analysis.

The first interpretation is a two-novel science fiction series authored by Tim C. Taylor . Published by Greyhart Press, the series consists of Book 1, *The Slough of Despond*, and Book 2, *The City of Destruction* . This literary work is explicitly framed as a modern allegory loosely inspired by John Bunyan's 1678 classic, *The Pilgrim’s Progress* . However, the series is described as embedding Bunyanesque motifs—such as a narrow path leading towards a celestial city analog—within complex frameworks of time travel, paradox, and alternate realities , . The narrative is geographically anchored in real locations in Bedfordshire, England, specifically the village of Elstow, which is tied to John Bunyan's life and writings . For instance, the story incorporates sites like Elstow Green, where Bunyan reportedly had a religious vision, and 'Bunyan’s Mead', a row of pre-17th-century cottages he would have passed daily . The series explores spiritual duality through mirror-image characters from rival realities and presents its themes as neither a Christian nor an anti-Christian allegory but rather as a speculative fiction exploration of these motifs . The first book, *The Slough of Despond*, was published on February 9, 2012, with Kindle and ePUB editions released at a launch price of 99 cents and 77 pence, respectively . The second book, *The City of Destruction*, followed with a Kindle release on July 9, 2012, and subsequent releases for other ePUB platforms like Barnes & Noble, iTunes, Sony, and Kobo on October 26, 2012 . While this novel series is a verifiable entity with specific publication data, it appears to be a niche literary work with no indication of extensive critical review or widespread cultural impact within the provided sources, limiting its notability compared to the other interpretations.

A third, more abstract interpretation exists within academic and policy discourse, though it lacks formal recognition as a definable event or concept. The phrase "The Reality War" is identified as an unattested variant or conflation of the widely discussed "information war" trope . It is not a documented historical event, organization, or a concept found in authoritative publications under that exact title . Instead, it is described as a rhetorical framing used in media and policy discussions since at least 2016 to discuss issues of disinformation . Sources analyzing this usage critique the militarized metaphors inherent in such phrases, including "the (dis)information wars," "battle against disinformation," and "front lines of the (dis)information wars" . These critiques argue that such terminology creates unsound conceptual frameworks that obscure the root causes of misinformation, overemphasize individual actors (like self-proclaimed "Napoleons of the information war"), and falsely imply that the problem is a winnable, bounded conflict . No reliable source cited in the analysis uses the exact phrase "The Reality War" as a proper noun with definable entities, a timeline, or an authoritative treatment, confirming its status as a non-standard, connotative expression rather than a formal concept .

The most significant and well-documented interpretation is as the title of an episode of the British television program *Doctor Who*. Specifically, it refers to the eighteenth episode of the second series of the show's revival, which aired as the season finale on May 31, 2025 , . This episode is produced under the leadership of Russell T Davies, marking his second tenure as showrunner, often referred to as the 'RTD2' era . The episode is part of a two-part story arc that began with the previous episode, 'Wish World' . As a major installment in one of the world's longest-running science fiction franchises, the episode attracted significant attention from fans and media outlets alike, making it a subject of considerable notability. Its narrative, particularly its controversial conclusion involving a Doctor's regeneration, generated widespread discussion and debate, ensuring its place as a prominent cultural event , . The depth of available information regarding its production, plot, cast, and reception makes it the most suitable and comprehensive subject for a detailed encyclopedic article. The following sections of this report will therefore focus exclusively on the *Doctor Who* episode, using the other interpretations only to establish context for the ambiguity of the title itself.

## Production and Context

The television episode titled "The Reality War" was produced as the concluding chapter of the second series of the *Doctor Who* revival, starring Ncuti Gatwa as the Fifteenth Doctor , . Aired on May 31, 2025, the episode served as the season finale, bringing to a close the tenure of showrunner Russell T Davies during his second stint on the series , , . The production was a collaborative effort between BBC Studios and Bad Wolf, operating under a co-production agreement between the BBC and Disney , , . This partnership was a crucial element of the show's recent history, providing the financial backing necessary for the high-budget spectacle characteristic of the modern *Doctor Who* era. The script for the episode was written by Russell T Davies himself and is copyrighted by the BBC, designated for private personal use only and prohibited from distribution or AI training without formal rights clearance . This copyright notice also includes a caveat that scripts may contain outdated or offensive language reflective of their writing date .

The production team included Alex Sanjiv Pillai and Ben A Williams as credited directors for the episode . The music was composed by Murray Gold, a frequent contributor to the series known for his iconic theme and score for the revived era . The episode featured a diverse ensemble cast portraying a mix of established characters and new arrivals, all integral to the complex narrative. The Fifteenth Doctor, played by Ncuti Gatwa, is the protagonist of the series and the central figure whose actions drive the plot's resolution , . He is joined by companions Ruby Sunday, played by Millie Gibson, and Belinda Chandra, portrayed by Varada Sethu , . Other key recurring characters include the Rani, an arch-enemy of the Doctor, portrayed by Archie Panjabi; Mrs. Flood, another recurring antagonist, played by Anita Dobson; and Conrad Clark, a companion from a parallel reality, played by Jonah Hauer-King , . The plot also involved Omega, a powerful Time Lord villain with whom the Doctor has a long-standing history, with the voice of Nicholas Briggs reprising the role , . The episode notably featured Mel, a former companion, played by Bonnie Langford, and made a canonical crossover appearance with the Thirteenth Doctor, Jodie Whittaker, marking their first on-screen pairing outside of the Fugitive Doctor storyline , . The casting of Billie Piper, who reprises her role as Rose Tyler, added a layer of immense complexity and controversy to the episode's production and reception , .

The broadcast of "The Reality War" occurred at a period of significant uncertainty for the future of the *Doctor Who* franchise. The BBC had officially announced a hiatus for the show, pending decisions from Disney regarding its commitment to the ongoing co-production partnership . This created a sense of impending change and potential discontinuation, which contextualized the episode's function as both a narrative climax and a potential series finale , . The announcement of the hiatus left many questions unanswered, contributing to a climate of anxiety among the fanbase about the show's future direction and the fate of its current cast . The episode's narrative, centered on themes of reality manipulation, wish fulfillment, and temporal collapse, was thus viewed against the backdrop of a real-world crisis for the show's continuity and funding. The production's reliance on the BBC-Disney deal meant that the episode's success or failure, both critically and commercially, carried heightened importance for the survival of the series. The involvement of Russell T Davies, a pivotal figure in the show's modern revival, further amplified the stakes, as his departure or the end of his tenure signaled a potential end to an era , .

The high-profile writers, directors, and cast, combined with the significant commercial pressures and uncertain future of the franchise, created a unique environment in which "The Reality War" was conceived, filmed, and ultimately broadcast. The episode's narrative choices cannot be fully appreciated without considering these underlying production realities.

## Plot Summary

The plot of "The Reality War" unfolds as a complex, multi-layered narrative that combines elements of time travel, reality manipulation, and family drama, culminating in a shocking and controversial resolution. The story begins as a direct continuation of the preceding episode, 'Wish World', and centers on a group of characters trapped in a persistent temporal loop fixed on Friday, March 23rd , . The central catalyst for the episode's events is a "magic baby" named Poppy, born from a human/Time Lord hybrid DNA . Poppy is the product of a wish made by Conrad Clark in his parallel reality, a dystopian "tradwife" world where women are subservient and men hold absolute power . When Conrad wished for a child, the universe interpreted his desire literally, creating Poppy, a being of immense psychic power capable of reshaping reality itself , .

The main characters find themselves drawn into this escalating crisis. The Fifteenth Doctor, along with his companions Ruby and Belinda, arrives in Conrad's world just as it collapses after he wishes for a normal life, causing Poppy to vanish from existence . To prevent this, the Doctor must intervene, channeling regeneration energy into the TARDIS' Time Vortex to shift reality by a mere 1%, a desperate measure designed to stabilize Poppy and save her from vanishing when the Wish World collapses . This act of cosmic recalibration sets off a chain of events that forces the characters to confront their deepest desires and fears. The Rani, seeking to exploit Poppy's reality-warping abilities for her own ends, and Mrs. Flood, acting as an enigmatic guide and antagonist, add further layers of conflict , . Meanwhile, Omega, the ancient and powerful Time Lord, reappears, threatening to reshape Earth into a "neocon world" using a device repurposed from a simple tracking tool into a galaxy-scale weapon , .

The narrative weaves together these disparate threads, exploring themes of motherhood, identity, and the nature of reality. Belinda Chandra, a character who has struggled with autonomy and boundaries throughout the series, finds herself retroactively and unconsentedly designated as Poppy's lifelong mother through a sonic scan performed by the Doctor . This abrupt alteration of her character arc becomes a focal point of the episode's later controversy. The story reaches its climax when the Doctor, facing the imminent destruction of Poppy and the unraveling of reality, makes a monumental sacrifice. After channeling regeneration energy to stabilize the baby, he allows his body to regenerate, transforming into the likeness of Billie Piper's character, Rose Tyler , . This marks the first time a former companion has assumed the role of the Doctor, a radical departure from established continuity . In this new incarnation, the Sixteenth Doctor is able to resolve the temporal loops, defeat the Rani and Omega, and restore balance, effectively putting a definitive end to the events of the episode , . The Thirteenth Doctor, Jodie Whittaker's character, makes a brief appearance to lend her support, creating a canonical crossover moment that solidifies the resolution , .

The plot's intricate design involves several key pieces of technology and lore from the *Doctor Who* universe. The Vindicator device, originally used for tracking, is shown to be capable of far greater destructive power when manipulated correctly . The concept of bi-generation, where a Doctor regenerates into another person, is introduced as a new form of regeneration, albeit one with significant implications for the show's continuity . The episode also revisits and expands upon prior canonical appearances, such as Omega's characterizations in the 1973 serial 'The Three Doctors' and the 1983 serial 'Arc of Infinity' . The narrative's foundation in time travel paradoxes and alternate realities provides a rich framework for the story's speculative elements, even as its ultimate solution—a regeneration into a companion—strays significantly from traditional storytelling methods in the franchise , . The plot's progression, from a localized temporal anomaly to a universe-threatening crisis resolved by a single, unprecedented act of regeneration, demonstrates the high stakes and dramatic intensity characteristic of the series' season finales.

## Critical Reception and Fan Reaction

The broadcast of "The Reality War" on May 31, 2025, elicited a polarized and intense response from critics and the viewing public, characterized by widespread controversy and strong negative reactions , . The episode's narrative choices, particularly its handling of established characters and its climactic resolution, were met with significant backlash, sparking debates across social media, news outlets, and fan communities , . The central plot twist—the Fifteenth Doctor's regeneration into Billie Piper's Rose Tyler—was the primary source of contention, with many viewers expressing concerns over its impact on canon integrity and its perceived prioritization of nostalgia over originality , . Major media outlets reported on the controversy, highlighting the deep divide within the fanbase regarding the creative direction of the show under Russell T Davies . The episode's reception was further complicated by the broader context of the show's uncertain future, as Disney's potential withdrawal from the BBC-Disney co-production agreement loomed over the entire season , .

Critics pointed to several aspects of the episode as narratively incoherent and thematically underdeveloped . The abrupt abandonment of established character arcs and villains was a frequently cited point of criticism. For example, the episode was criticized for discarding the dramatic weight of major antagonists like the Rani and Omega, who were defeated without a satisfying confrontation, and for resolving Conrad's dystopian "tradwife" reality by having Ruby simply wish him away without any accountability for his actions . The handling of Belinda Chandra's character was particularly contentious, with critics describing the retroactive imposition of a motherhood role via an unconsented sonic scan as a violation of her previously established autonomy and boundary-setting from earlier episodes . Robert Shearman, the acclaimed writer of the 2005 episode 'Dalek', weighed in on the episode's impact, stating in *Doctor Who Magazine* that "The Reality War" effectively "put a full stop on things," framing its closing moments as a definitive endpoint for the series rather than a launchpad for future stories . This sentiment reflected a broader feeling among some critics that the episode's creative choices represented a form of "creative cowardice" that prioritized shock value and nostalgia over continuity integrity and original storytelling .

Despite the critical backlash, the episode's star-studded cast and the novelty of Billie Piper's return undoubtedly drew a large audience. However, viewership figures presented a mixed picture that contributed to the overall unease surrounding the series. Official BARB seven-day viewing figures for the season reported an average audience of 3.2 million viewers across the eight episodes, a decrease of 500,000 from the previous season . More alarmingly, the episode immediately preceding "The Reality War" drew just 1.5 million overnight UK viewers, the smallest audience in the show's 61-year history, following a record low of 1.58 million in the prior week . While the season average remained respectable, these drops indicated a significant decline in live viewership, fueling speculation about the show's appeal and its ability to attract new audiences amidst a changing media landscape , .

The fan reaction was immediate and vocal. The BBC's decision to publish a headline on its news website stating "Ncuti Gatwa regenerates into Billie Piper as he leaves Doctor Who" shortly after the broadcast prompted numerous viewer complaints about spoilers . The corporation acknowledged the feedback, updated the headline to clarify Gatwa's regeneration into Piper, added a spoiler alert to the article body, and committed to being "more mindful" of spoiler handling in the future . This incident underscored the sensitivity of the topic and the power of the fanbase to influence corporate communications. The controversy surrounding Billie Piper's return remains unresolved, with the BBC issuing a vague post-air statement—"Just how and why she is back remains to be seen"—and Russell T Davies offering a similarly cryptic quote, leaving her official status as the Sixteenth Doctor as a matter of ongoing speculation . Piper herself confirmed her return, stating in a direct quote that she "couldn’t refuse" the opportunity to re-enter the Whoniverse, but the specifics of her role remain unconfirmed as of the episode's airing . This combination of critical condemnation, declining viewership, and a deeply divided fanbase cemented "The Reality War" as one of the most talked-about and controversial episodes in recent *Doctor Who* history.

## Controversy and Canon Integrity

The primary controversy surrounding "The Reality War" stems from its perceived disregard for established canon and its controversial narrative resolutions, which many critics and fans felt undermined the integrity of the *Doctor Who* universe , . The episode's creative decisions were widely interpreted as a form of "creative cowardice" that prioritized nostalgic callbacks and shocking twists over thoughtful, coherent storytelling . A central point of contention was the abrupt and seemingly arbitrary alteration of character arcs, most notably that of Belinda Chandra. Throughout the series, Belinda had been developed as a character asserting her independence and setting firm boundaries with the Doctor and Ruby . In "The Reality War," however, her identity is retroactively overwritten when the Fifteenth Doctor unilaterally scans her and declares her to be the lifelong mother of the "magic baby," Poppy, without her consent or input . This move was condemned by critics as a narrative shortcut that erased years of character development in favor of a convenient plot device, fundamentally betraying the character's established personality and agency .

Similarly, the handling of major antagonists was a significant source of fan frustration. The Rani and Omega, both formidable and long-standing enemies of the Doctor, were dispatched with little dramatic weight or conclusive victory . Their defeat felt perfunctory, lacking the epic scale and narrative satisfaction expected of encounters with such iconic villains. This was contrasted with the resolution of the more minor threat posed by Conrad Clark's "Wish World." His dystopian reality, which explored troubling themes of misogyny and authoritarianism, was resolved not through a confrontation or a meaningful choice, but by having Ruby simply wish him away, absolving him of any responsibility for the consequences of his actions . Critics argued that this approach demonstrated a thematic laziness, avoiding the difficult work of exploring the real-world implications of the ideas presented in the story . The episode's overarching narrative was thus seen by some as a patchwork of discarded elements, failing to give proper closure to any of its conflicts and instead opting for a simplistic, emotionally manipulative resolution .

The episode's climactic regeneration of the Fifteenth Doctor into Billie Piper's Rose Tyler stands as the most divisive aspect of its plot and a lightning rod for controversy over canon . While Piper's return was a major draw for many fans, the manner in which it was executed was widely criticized as a breach of fundamental rules within the *Doctor Who* mythos . The regeneration of a Time Lord into a human companion is a concept that defies established lore, raising questions about the mechanics of Time Lord biology and the nature of regeneration itself. The ambiguity surrounding Piper's official status further fueled the debate; the vague statements from the BBC and Russell T Davies left fans questioning whether she was truly the Sixteenth Doctor or a separate entity entirely . This lack of clarity, coupled with the episode's other controversial choices, led to a crisis of trust among the audience. Many felt that the creative team had abandoned the careful, consistent world-building that has been a hallmark of the show for decades in favor of a spectacle-driven narrative that prioritized celebrity recasting over narrative coherence , . The episode's legacy is therefore deeply intertwined with this controversy, representing a moment where the franchise's past and present collided in a way that alienated a significant portion of its audience and raised serious questions about the future of its storytelling traditions.

## Legacy and Future Implications

The legacy of "The Reality War" is multifaceted, defined by its profound impact on the *Doctor Who* franchise, its lasting effect on the perception of its creators, and its reflection of the challenges facing long-running media properties in the modern entertainment landscape. Broadcast as the season finale of Russell T Davies' second tenure as showrunner, the episode's controversial nature overshadowed the conclusion of the season and cast a long shadow over the series' future , . The intense fan and critical backlash, coupled with documented declines in viewership, placed the show at a crossroads, forcing a reckoning with its narrative priorities and its relationship with its audience , . The episode's legacy is therefore not merely a footnote in the series' history but a defining moment that encapsulates the tensions between creative ambition, commercial viability, and fan expectations.

Perhaps the most significant implication of "The Reality War" is the uncertainty it introduced into the future of *Doctor Who*. The episode aired amid an official hiatus announced by the BBC, directly linked to Disney's indecision regarding its commitment to the BBC-Disney co-production agreement , . This created a precarious situation where the show's very existence was in question. The controversial ending, with Ncuti Gatwa's abbreviated 18-month tenure as the Fifteenth Doctor and the abrupt regeneration into Billie Piper, made the series feel more fragile than ever , . The unresolved status of Piper's return added another layer of ambiguity, with the creative team providing few answers beyond cryptic quotes from Russell T Davies . This period of uncertainty transformed the episode from a simple season finale into a potential swansong, a dramatic and divisive conclusion to an era that left the door open for a new beginning, but only if the commercial and creative partners could agree on a path forward , . The legacy of the episode is thus inseparable from the existential questions it helped to raise about the show's next chapter.

In retrospect, "The Reality War" serves as a case study in the complexities of managing a beloved, long-running intellectual property. The attempt to blend spectacular, high-concept sci-fi with potent emotional storytelling and a nostalgic return for a popular actress resulted in a narrative that many felt was narratively incoherent and disrespectful to established continuity , . The backlash highlighted a fundamental tension within the franchise: the desire to innovate and surprise the audience versus the obligation to honor the rich tapestry of lore and character development built over six decades. The episode's legacy is a cautionary tale about the risks of prioritizing shock value and celebrity appeal over the meticulous craft of storytelling that has sustained *Doctor Who*'s popularity. Ultimately, "The Reality War" will likely be remembered as a pivotal and polarizing episode that forced a conversation about the soul of the series, a conversation that will undoubtedly continue as the franchise navigates its uncertain future.

The Thirteenth Doctor, Jodie Whittaker's character, makes a brief appearance to lend her support, creating a canonical crossover moment that solidifies the resolution.
The plot's intricate design involves several key pieces of technology and lore from the *Doctor Who* universe.
The Vindicator device, originally used for tracking, is shown to be capable of far greater destructive power when manipulated correctly.
The concept of bi-generation, where a Doctor regenerates into another person, is introduced as a new form of regeneration, albeit one with significant implications for the show's continuity.
The episode also revisits and expands upon prior canonical appearances, such as Omega's characterizations in the 1973 serial 'The Three Doctors' and the 1983 serial 'Arc of Infinity'.

The narrative's foundation in time travel paradoxes and alternate realities provides a rich framework for the story's speculative elements, even as its ultimate solution—a regeneration into a companion—strays significantly from traditional storytelling methods in the franchise.

The plot's progression, from a localized temporal anomaly to a universe-threatening crisis resolved by a single, unprecedented act of regeneration, demonstrates the high stakes and dramatic intensity characteristic of the series' season finales.

The broadcast of "The Reality War" on May 31, 2025, elicited a polarized and intense response from critics and the viewing public, characterized by widespread controversy and strong negative reactions.

The episode's narrative choices, particularly its handling of established characters and its climactic resolution, were met with significant backlash, sparking debates across social media, news outlets, and fan communities.

The central plot twist—the Fifteenth Doctor's regeneration into Billie Piper's Rose Tyler—was the primary source of contention, with many viewers expressing concerns over its impact on canon integrity and its perceived prioritization of nostalgia over originality.
Major media outlets reported on the controversy, highlighting the deep divide within the fanbase regarding the creative direction of the show under Russell T Davies.

The episode's reception was further complicated by the broader context of the show's uncertain future, as Disney's potential withdrawal from the BBC-Disney co-production agreement loomed over the entire season.
Critics pointed to several aspects of the episode as narratively incoherent and thematically underdeveloped.
The abrupt abandonment of established character arcs and villains was a frequently cited point of criticism.

For example, the episode was criticized for discarding the dramatic weight of major antagonists like the Rani and Omega, who were defeated without a satisfying confrontation, and for resolving Conrad's dystopian "tradwife" reality by having Ruby simply wish him away without any accountability for his actions.

The handling of Belinda Chandra's character was particularly contentious, with critics describing the retroactive imposition of a motherhood role via an unconsented sonic scan as a violation of her previously established autonomy and boundary-setting from earlier episodes.

Robert Shearman, the acclaimed writer of the 2005 episode 'Dalek', weighed in on the episode's impact, stating in *Doctor Who Magazine* that "The Reality War" effectively "put a full stop on things," framing its closing moments as a definitive endpoint for the series rather than a launchpad for future stories.

This sentiment reflected a broader feeling among some critics that the episode's creative choices represented a form of "creative cowardice" that prioritized shock value and nostalgia over continuity integrity and original storytelling.
Despite the critical backlash, the episode's star-studded cast and the novelty of Billie Piper's return undoubtedly drew a large audience.
However, viewership figures presented a mixed picture that contributed to the overall unease surrounding the series.
Official BARB seven-day viewing figures for the season reported an average audience of 3.2 million viewers across the eight episodes, a decrease of 500,000 from the previous season.

More alarmingly, the episode immediately preceding "The Reality War" drew just 1.5 million overnight UK viewers, the smallest audience in the show's 61-year history, following a record low of 1.58 million in the prior week.

While the season average remained respectable, these drops indicated a significant decline in live viewership, fueling speculation about the show's appeal and its ability to attract new audiences amidst a changing media landscape.
The fan reaction was immediate and vocal.

The BBC's decision to publish a headline on its news website stating "Ncuti Gatwa regenerates into Billie Piper as he leaves Doctor Who" shortly after the broadcast prompted numerous viewer complaints about spoilers.

The corporation acknowledged the feedback, updated the headline to clarify Gatwa's regeneration into Piper, added a spoiler alert to the article body, and committed to being "more mindful" of spoiler handling in the future.
This incident underscored the sensitivity of the topic and the power of the fanbase to influence corporate communications.

The controversy surrounding Billie Piper's return remains unresolved, with the BBC issuing a vague post-air statement—"Just how and why she is back remains to be seen"—and Russell T Davies offering a similarly cryptic quote, leaving her official status as the Sixteenth Doctor as a matter of ongoing speculation.

Piper herself confirmed her return, stating in a direct quote that she "couldn’t refuse" the opportunity to re-enter the Whoniverse, but the specifics of her role remain unconfirmed as of the episode's airing.

This combination of critical condemnation, declining viewership, and a deeply divided fanbase cemented "The Reality War" as one of the most talked-about and controversial episodes in recent *Doctor Who* history.

The primary controversy surrounding "The Reality War" stems from its perceived disregard for established canon and its controversial narrative resolutions, which many critics and fans felt undermined the integrity of the *Doctor Who* universe.
The episode's creative decisions were widely interpreted as a form of "creative cowardice" that prioritized nostalgic callbacks and shocking twists over thoughtful, coherent storytelling.
A central point of contention was the abrupt and seemingly arbitrary alteration of character arcs, most notably that of Belinda Chandra.
Throughout the series, Belinda had been developed as a character asserting her independence and setting firm boundaries with the Doctor and Ruby.

In "The Reality War," however, her identity is retroactively overwritten when the Fifteenth Doctor unilaterally scans her and declares her to be the lifelong mother of the "magic baby," Poppy, without her consent or input.

This move was condemned by critics as a narrative shortcut that erased years of character development in favor of a convenient plot device, fundamentally betraying the character's established personality and agency.
Similarly, the handling of major antagonists was a significant source of fan frustration.
The Rani and Omega, both formidable and long-standing enemies of the Doctor, were dispatched with little dramatic weight or conclusive victory.
Their defeat felt perfunctory, lacking the epic scale and narrative satisfaction expected of encounters with such iconic villains.
This was contrasted with the resolution of the more minor threat posed by Conrad Clark's "Wish World."

His dystopian reality, which explored troubling themes of misogyny and authoritarianism, was resolved not through a confrontation or a meaningful choice, but by having Ruby simply wish him away, absolving him of any responsibility for the consequences of his actions.
Critics argued that this approach demonstrated a thematic laziness, avoiding the difficult work of exploring the real-world implications of the ideas presented in the story.

The episode's overarching narrative was thus seen by some as a patchwork of discarded elements, failing to give proper closure to any of its conflicts and instead opting for a simplistic, emotionally manipulative resolution.
The episode's climactic regeneration of the Fifteenth Doctor into Billie Piper's Rose Tyler stands as the most divisive aspect of its plot and a lightning rod for controversy over canon.
While Piper's return was a major draw for many fans, the manner in which it was executed was widely criticized as a breach of fundamental rules within the *Doctor Who* mythos.
The regeneration of a Time Lord into a human companion is a concept that defies established lore, raising questions about the mechanics of Time Lord biology and the nature of regeneration itself.

The ambiguity surrounding Piper's official status further fueled the debate; the vague statements from the BBC and Russell T Davies left fans questioning whether she was truly the Sixteenth Doctor or a separate entity entirely.
This lack of clarity, coupled with the episode's other controversial choices, led to a crisis of trust among the audience.

Many felt that the creative team had abandoned the careful, consistent world-building that has been a hallmark of the show for decades in favor of a spectacle-driven narrative that prioritized celebrity recasting over narrative coherence.

The episode's legacy is therefore deeply intertwined with this controversy, representing a moment where the franchise's past and present collided in a way that alienated a significant portion of its audience and raised serious questions about the future of its storytelling traditions.

The legacy of "The Reality War" is multifaceted, defined by its profound impact on the *Doctor Who* franchise, its lasting effect on the perception of its creators, and its reflection of the challenges facing long-running media properties in the modern entertainment landscape.

Broadcast as the season finale of Russell T Davies' second tenure as showrunner, the episode's controversial nature overshadowed the conclusion of the season and cast a long shadow over the series' future.

The intense fan and critical backlash, coupled with documented declines in viewership, placed the show at a crossroads, forcing a reckoning with its narrative priorities and its relationship with its audience.

The episode's legacy is therefore not merely a footnote in the series' history but a defining moment that encapsulates the tensions between creative ambition, commercial viability, and fan expectations.
Perhaps the most significant implication of "The Reality War" is the uncertainty it introduced into the future of *Doctor Who*.
The episode aired amid an official hiatus announced by the BBC, directly linked to Disney's indecision regarding its commitment to the BBC-Disney co-production agreement.
This created a precarious situation where the show's very existence was in question.
The controversial ending, with Ncuti Gatwa's abbreviated 18-month tenure as the Fifteenth Doctor and the abrupt regeneration into Billie Piper, made the series feel more fragile than ever.
The unresolved status of Piper's return added another layer of ambiguity, with the creative team providing few answers beyond cryptic quotes from Russell T Davies.

This period of uncertainty transformed the episode from a simple season finale into a potential swansong, a dramatic and divisive conclusion to an era that left the door open for a new beginning, but only if the commercial and creative partners could agree on a path forward.
The legacy of the episode is thus inseparable from the existential questions it helped to raise about the show's next chapter.
In retrospect, "The Reality War" serves as a case study in the complexities of managing a beloved, long-running intellectual property.

The attempt to blend spectacular, high-concept sci-fi with potent emotional storytelling and a nostalgic return for a popular actress resulted in a narrative that many felt was narratively incoherent and disrespectful to established continuity.

The backlash highlighted a fundamental tension within the franchise: the desire to innovate and surprise the audience versus the obligation to honor the rich tapestry of lore and character development built over six decades.
The episode's legacy is a cautionary tale about the risks of prioritizing shock value and celebrity appeal over the meticulous craft of storytelling that has sustained *Doctor Who*'s popularity.

Ultimately, "The Reality War" will likely be remembered as a pivotal and polarizing episode that forced a conversation about the soul of the series, a conversation that will undoubtedly continue as the franchise navigates its uncertain future.

May 31, 2025

[The Reality War Review](https://www.eruditorumpress.com/blog/the-reality-war-review)
=====================================================================================

[Elizabeth Sandifer](https://www.eruditorumpress.com/blog/author/elizabeth) [](https://www.eruditorumpress.com/blog/category/uncategorized)[200](https://www.eruditorumpress.com/blog/the-reality-war-review#comments)

![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.eruditorumpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/reality2.jpg?resize=501%2C282&ssl=1)

We spent so much time thinking that a better world was possible that we forgot to consider that a worse one was too.

It’s always useful to take stock of where you are, so hey. It’s May 31st, 2025. I think I read that Morgan Wallen is at number one. But never mind that. On television, Doctor Who has just lurched into an uncertain non-existence, there’s a trailer for the Sea Devil spinoff, and we just Introduced Billie Piper, though pointedly not as the Doctor. The episode was wholly embargoed for a genuine world wide premiere, and so I’m reacting in real time with the rest of the world in attempting to process this hourlong piece of television that just happened to me.

Broadly, in terms of this precise moment, I think I liked it. I could not begin to predict what I will think about it at any other time in my life. But that’s future El’s problem. I’ve gotta get a review out, and I broadly liked it. If it is, in fact, the last episode of Doctor Who, it ended like I feel about that: in a sense of subtle wrongness. I even, perversely, find myself liking _Wish World_ more, in that it extends the wrongness. There’s a fractal perfection to it—here we are, trapped in an apocalyptic hell world in which the rotting soul of the twentieth century genocides trans people, just like on TV.

And like, I can do so much with this. Cause, see, the fascist on TV peers out from the screen just like Patrick Troughton, and the Underverse is Narnia, and there’s fucking Susan. I’ve not gone frame by frame through, but I think Yasmin Finney disappears from the episode once reality starts breaking, and then we get the Doctor regenerating into Rose. Like, my conspiracy wall on this shit is _huge_. I’m gonna Eruditorum the shit out of this someday.

But right now, in the moment, all I know is that I’ve definitely never seen anything like that. Up to the halfway point or so, it is simply the sugar rush thrill of _Journey’s End_—the repeated fireworks as bits of continuity and fanwank are rolled out in perfectly escalating order. Bonnie Langford’s entrance to UNIT HQ is particularly immaculate, and delightfully paid off in her sneering hatred of the Rani, which she plays with startling intensity. ”We meet again” is clearly a line Bonnie Langford has waited her career for. The story fragments into three well-defined arcs for the three credit-level characters. Each strand gets some great moments: that sharp cut to Belinda in the zero chamber, the furious precision with which Ruby dismantles Conrad’s defenses, and the Doctor’s delighted “fuck yeah” to seeing Omega (because of course he does), all of them just starting points for some great sequences.

Then at the halfway point the Doctor smoothly plucks the Vindicator out of his bag of unresolved setups and shoots Zombie Omega, and we enter the far more puzzling back half—a series of “gosh, there’s sure a lot of episode left” cliffhangers that gradually drift askance, repeatedly not quite getting reality back together into a configuration that can possibly feel like a resolution. These too are precisely delivered—Whittaker slipping through the narrative cracks of the moment to have the Yaz subplot and her emotional unavailability highlighted is a particular treat, as is the meta-dialogue about how if they get this wrong the show will be cancelled. But they repeatedly move the story away from the path it ostentatiously flagged for itself—the one that goes and resolves the giant knot of emotional/continuity trauma around the Doctor, parenthood, and Susan. At times this is genuinely disorienting—the Doctor and Belinda forgetting about Poppy and preparing to spin off on endless travels is a remarkable piece of sustained dissonance. And then like, the narrative collapses so hard reality shatters and the Doctor orgasmically regenerates into Billie Piper and the credits roll and we wait to find out what Disney is doing and wonder if we’ll live til Christmas 2026 or whenever we actually come back.

And I ask myself, what if this is _Survival_ redux? You can pretty much see the join, after all—somewhere in or around the last UNIT scene, when it pivots awkwardly to being a regeneration story instead the originally shot ending that presumably had Carole Ann Ford in it. So did Davies slap a weird coda onto his show as effectively as Cartmel dashed up “worlds out there where the sky’s burning?” If this is it for Doctor Who, is it a good ending? And ultimately I think yes. I don’t want Doctor Who to end, and I broadly appreciate Davies for seemingly going out of his way to end on a sour, unsatisfying cliffhanger. It’s as if the show is as annoyed as I am about this renewal bulshit, as if the story desperately wants to go on and is stuck at a red light that won’t turn. In which case, well done Davies. We’re all on the same page.

And if there is more? Well, I suppose we’ll see. I remain genuinely interested in the idea of engaging meaningfully with Susan. Billie Piper as the Doctor is superficially alarming but also something that could perfectly plausibly work—it’s not as if she’s a bad actress. I want to know what we’re doing with Anita Dobson notably surviving and Boss and all those random unfired guns on the mantelpiece. Maybe it’ll all be complete rubbish. Maybe it’ll get cancelled after twenty-three years and seventeen seasons, a run almost as impressive as the first time. Maybe it’ll resolve the Timeless Child in earnest. Maybe that was just it. We’ll see.

But this is today, and I have to decide what I thought of this weird two-parter and rank it on a list with the rest of the season. Suppose I’d better get to bullet points.

*   The Rani finally manages to settle as a character for me here. It’s the sneering superiority of being a Time Lord—her cackling eugenics about the inferiority of humanity and Time Lord racial superiority—that finally cements it. Rani as Peter Thiel technofascist. That works. That’s solid.
*   I’m also charmed by the Panjabi version just getting eaten as soon as she accomplishes her plan. The degree to which she’s comical and low rent is really carefully calculated, with Mrs. Flood successfully remaining as the more plausibly interesting version. 
*   Also the entire “I’ll do anything for you mistress” scene with Conrad was absolutely bonkers. Who expected Davies to out-horny Moffat. 
*   Speaking of whom, utterly charmed by Anita being the deus ex machina to resolve the cliffhanger. Less charmed by the Joy to the World callback in the regeneration (although “this has been an absolute joy” was sweet). But I do like that Moffat bails Davies out of his narrative collapse.
*   OK, fanwank corner. First of all, I like the vague stabilization of the second Time Lord genocide. The hazily defined “genetic explosion” that kills all the Time Lords except for the ones it doesn’t, and sterilizes the rest is actually a thematically sane interpretation of _The Timeless Children_. Second of all, I’m horribly amused by Chibnall’s half-baked adoption trauma stuff becoming the excuse to go full Curse of the Pythia. But third of all, and most significantly, _did they just fucking solve UNIT dating_?
*   Comments all season have been quite divided on Belinda. I quite like her. The dichotomy of being a perfectly capable companion who can see the appeal of the Doctor and someone who urgently doesn’t want to be there is a solid character concept, and has been since the days of Jacqueline Hill. Sethu does a bang-up job of playing her, and the result holds together. It’s simple and efficient as concepts go. 
*   Ruby remains more complicated, and not just in her seeming status as a semi-permanent feature of the UNIT landscape. I can’t really say that character ever fully clicks, even as Millie Gibson can deliver individual scenes when called to, but the whole never quite gelled.
*   Honestly, there’s a degree to which that’s how I feel about the Gatwa era. Penn and I were listening to Serpentwithfeet’s _Grip_ the other day. There’s a lyric in one of the songs, “A penny saved might be a penny earned / But if you save that freaky shit for later, you’ll never learn.” And I noted that was basically how I thought of the Gatwa era. Obviously Gatwa himself is good. And there are oceans of potential in the openly libidinal Doctor—potential that periodically spills out into the actual episodes. But on the whole he feels like an unrealized opportunity. He didn’t even meet the Daleks. 
*   Right. the ranking. So, Penn wrote back in [_Liber Forty_](https://www.eruditorumpress.com/blog/liber-forty) about his wish magic. And obviously, I’m a supportive wife, so I joined in. After all, he’s wishing for the life we live together. Why wouldn’t I use whatever wishes I have to help sustain that? So I do. Every time I get an opportunity to wish, I wish for more time with him. Because like Jodie Whittaker of all fucking people says, you always do. And it’s hard not to think about that when looking at a Doctor Who finale that is in a large part about wishes. Especially when that finale has a backdrop of a fascist world in which trans people are literally erased. It’s just very on the nose.
*   I’ve talked about my suicidal ideation before. Usually a bit jokingly—I think I noted that the Whittaker era spiked it, which is tremendously petty. But it’s not entirely untrue, because that ideation is just sort of a constant background hum. I am, at the end of the day, inordinately tempted by antinatalism. And my dopamine system is a cratering wreck of ADHD so I’ve got chronic anhedonia, and I just think being alive in this world is a raw deal. Donald Trump is President and AI slop is consuming the Internet and the planet is cooking and no matter how hard we wish some day either I or Penn are going to have to wake up without the other one and it’s awful. Why would anyone want this? 
*   But then, of course, I have my wishes. Because, like, I’ve had this bullshit depression for as long as I can remember. I’ve gotten used to deciding against it. And for a long time—since 2011 at least—one of my standard tools for shutting that line of thought down has been “well yeah, but don’t you want to see the next episode of Doctor Who?” And like, that’s not the only thing or even the main thing. But it’s a reliable thing—a solid way to reorient myself when I get unmoored, dust myself off, and get back to work. 
*   And part of that—not all of it, but part of it—is that I owe this show so much of my life. Not the survival of it—I’d have found other things. I did so through the whole Whittaker era after all. But the facts of it. That wish I make isn’t just for Penn but for our life creating art. And the reason I have that, at the end of the day, is that I wrote a stupidly successful Doctor Who blog. 
*   Which, I’d be remiss if I didn’t use this opportunity to thank our Patrons one more time. Currently I’m pleased to say that the Patreon is actually at the level where I’ll do public _War Between the Land and Sea_ reviews whenever that airs. And after the weekend I’ll be getting back to _Last War in Albion_ v4, which hits _From Hell_ soon. They’ve also got a mid-size essay I wrote on Alan Turing and AI, and my commentary on _The Marriage of Heaven and Hell_, both of which I used the last eight weeks to write. And of course when I finish the _Last War in Albion_ v2 revisions and get that book out, all Patrons will get it for free. [So please consider joining up there, not least cause it’s the only place I’m gonna be posting regularly until the fall.](https://www.patreon.com/c/elizabethsandifer)  
*   But if this is where we leave Doctor Who for sixteen years (because in these terms, at least, Paul McGann will never count), well, what can I say. I still want more. I want to know where this daft cluster of ideas resolves. I want to know what the fuck Billie Piper as the Doctor is going to do. I want to see if Davies can actually land it, and I want to see what comes after him. I want more. Of Doctor Who, of Penn, of writing for our Patrons, all of it. I want more. And I don’t really know what more a girl can wish for than that.

**Rankings**

1.  Lux
2.  The Story and the Engine
3.  Wish World/The Reality War
4.  Joy to the World
5.  Lucky Day
6.  The Interstellar Song Contest
7.  The Well

    Letting this percolate, but I think the narrative collapse here is doing something very clever and profound in a way that utterly subverts the entire story that it looks like RTD is giving to us, through the Rani.
    
    Because she’s trying to access Omega, First Time Lord, through inducing her own narrative collapse of Doctor Who, reaching into the collective subconscious and pulling him out to reconstitute the Time Lord race, only better. And in doing that, she quite literally stands in front of the Doctor, of all people, and quite literally has another character ask why his and her DNA wouldn’t suffice to reconstitute the Time Lords, and rejects the very idea. And yet, her solution, while profoundly queer, is also profoundly conservative and reactionary: she wants to Make Gallifrey Great Again. Of course she wants to bring back the First of the Race to do that. And of course what she brings back out of the Underverse bears little resemblance either to the man Omega, or what remained of him to appear on screen in two previous stories: a fetal corpse, an artifact that would produce the Time Lords purely to consume them, the Mad God everyone built Omega into, the object of collective dreams and delusions, a Dead End. Of course the Mad God eats her face (and the rest of her), eagerly: after all, isn’t that what she wanted? Of course the Doctor drives him away but cannot (and would not) end him.
    
    Because Omega isn’t the First of the Time Lords, not really. The Timeless Child implies that the Doctor was first, though the “lord” part didn’t really apply. And The Reality War suggests instead that we (and the Rani) are using the wrong model, the worst model: are we really claiming Omega (the end) as the Alpha of the Time Lords, and insisting on something ordinal and linear? Even the Time Lord society we saw in the show preferred cardinal to ordinal; Omega is only the Rani’s target because she is congenitally incapable of recognizing the Doctor as what she really should have been wishing for: Last of the Time Lords, maybe First, but more to the point, last multiple times, mixed up and out of order, striving (as the Rani accuses) to be “more than just another Time Lord” because in part the Doctor is drawn to humanity.
    
    Of course the Doctor is who you rebuild Time Lord society and Time Lord existence upon, because the Doctor (and the show) preceded the Time Lords. The Doctor’s origin isn’t Gallifrey because it follows from him, not vice versa: the planet and the people who lived there matter in the show because of the Doctor.
    
    And of course, set against the consuming and consumptive corpse of the Mad God, we have Gatwa’s Doctor, scrambled within his own timeline, sacrificing his life to nudge reality 1% over so that Poppy can live, despite the fact that by doing so, he loses a daughter he maybe never had, and possibly or possibly does not lose a granddaughter he always had but lost, and of course he maybe regenerates into Rose, or The Moment, or Bad Wolf, or whoever, because at this moment, in this episode, within the Reality War, the Doctor is the beginning and the end, the center of mavity, the Alpha as well as the Omega. “I live; I die; I live again” is cyclical, it is productive, it is generative. The Rani’s cliffhanger narrative collapse leads her up a blind alley; this episodes eventual narrative collapse is, at the moment, ongoing so long as Billie Piper’s status remains unclear, the show swallowing its own tail but not in a consumptive way but a regenerative one. I wouldn’t be surprised if Joy plus Regeneration didn’t bring back what was lost to the Flux (assuming Sutekh didn’t already do that); Susan Twist exists because of the Doctor, and so did Wilfred Mott, and Ruby Sunday, and all the other lives he saved.
    
    The Doctor may have had looked like he had a het baby in the last episode. But the child was produced asexually, via wish, ceased to exist shortly after the wish ended, and was then reproduced with this Doctor’s life (and some advice from Thirteen) in a form that left Poppy a life but a life distinct from the Doctor and legible as that het baby again. And yet… haven’t we seen the Doctor reproducing again and again, certainly since the first RTD series, through his companions, through the people he inspires, through the people he saves. He shines… and we can all aspire to be stars as a result.

Instead, the Doctor changed which reality _he_ was in, not reality itself. We know that the version post-wish of Belinda isn’t the Belinda he traveled with – she doesn’t want to go home, she doesn’t seem to care about getting back to her parents.     I’m seeing a lot of people annoyed about Poppy, on this site and elsewhere. The main argument seems to be that Belinda was forced to be a mother without her knowledge or consent. Maybe I’ve completely misunderstood the episode but that it not how I see it at all.
    
    I was thinking that the Doctor and Belinda (and by extension, we the viewers) have been in a false or incorrect reality all season. This is a reality where Poppy doesn’t exist and the world ends on 24 May 2025. I take it as given that any reality where the world ends (and this is not reversed) is not the ‘correct’ reality in Doctor Who. The world has somehow ended up in this other reality due to the Rani(s) and Conrad mucking about with reality itself. Although the Wish World isn’t fully formed until episode 7, it seems sensible that the events of the finale have repercussions backwards and forwards in time (e.g. see The Big Bang).
    
    So when Poppy appears in the Wish World (and the Story and the Engine), it is Belinda’s subconscious memory of the real or ‘correct’ reality bleeding through. So Belinda was a mother all along, she just didn’t know it (and neither did we). The Doctor’s sacrifice at the end is to shift time/reality so as not to settle for a ‘close enough’ reality, but to get back to the original version where Poppy always existed. Prior to this, it is acknowledged that the ‘close enough’ reality is not quite right – e.g. Ernest Borgnine is still alive, and the border or Norway and Sweden shifted etc.
    
    There is a deliberate sense of unease about this. When Poppy didn’t exist she _never_ existed and when she did exist, she _always_ had existed. It also isn’t clear why everyone can remember that Ernest Borgnine died etc but no one can remember Poppy, except Ruby. The Doctor is slightly evasive about fixing it. It should be noted (and it has been noted upthread) that Belinda is fully in support of the Doctor trying to get her daughter back, even though she can’t remember her. It feels disorienting at the end because the Belinda we end with is, by definition, not the same Belinda we saw all season. The character suffers from this (IMO). It also raises questions about how far back Reality has been affected – Season 1/14 as well? Is that why Poppy showed up in Space Babies? It all could have been set up better, granted.
    
    I dunno, I really think it is like Season 5, where Amy had no parents all season and didn’t notice anything was wrong, but at the end, when the cracks were fixed, her parents came back and she _always_ had parents.
    
    Maybe this is all just my head canon? I will re-watch one day (once I’ve had some separation from this era of Who) and get more out of it, perhaps. Incidentally, this is why WW/TRW is better than Power of the Doctor – as messy as this finale is, there’s enough depth and intentionality to support detailed analysis and multiple close readings.

        The fact that one can technically / Well, Actually one’s way out of Belinda being an unwilling mother doesn’t change how on a gut level it feels viscerally wrong to a lot of viewers (indeed, it seems to be the most widespread online reaction as far as I can tell). It’s absolutely true that the Hand of Authorly God writes it so that she’s determined to save Poppy’s life (though as Cyrano notes, nobody seems to care about the presumably thousands of other wish babies in ConradWorld who will also wink out of existence) and, indeed, that in itself is a fine beat, typical if slightly standard DW companion material to try and save a life. But the _choice_ (which is not necessitated by the motivation to save her life) to do a sharp heel turn and define her as A Mother First and Foremost is never not going to jar for a lot of people and create (ironically) the sort of unease you’re talking about wrt the childless timeline. It’s a hard sell to an audience that Wrong Timeline A as written by a villainous conservative is the one where she has a nice suburban life and a husband and a daughter and a tradwife existence and doesn’t go to work, as juxtaposed against Correct Timeline B, in which she’s a stressed and overworked nurse sharing a flat with others her age, except sike! Correct Timeline B is in fact Wrong Timeline B, and she really belongs in Correct Timeline C, in which she’s the overworked nurse from B but has the exact same suburban life/house from A and the same daughter from A but none of the obvious conservative fantasy trappings, and this has all come about because of the Doctor “nudging reality over” to make it happen, which comes uncomfortably close to a rewrite of the character as we knew her. As I say, one can Well, Actually the idea that the character we knew from the start was All Wrong and actually she was always a devoted mother, but if so one must be prepared for fierce pushback from people who think “fuck that” to such a starkly deterministic portrait of motherhood. _Functionally_, it is a rewrite, even if one can argue that it isn’t in-universe.
        
        What feels sketchy with where Belinda’s story ends up is slightly more than just “dodgy consensual issues around her timeline rewrite”, however. This is a character who began the season by fighting against the idea of dwelling in a reality being written by a problematic man who doesn’t listen to her. That is not the same person (more’s the pity) as the woman who happily accepts the reality at the end that’s been (re)written by a problematic man (one _explicitly paralleled_ to Alan from the start of this run, a parallel the finale never returns to) who doesn’t listen to her (he still calls her “Miss Belinda Chandra” at the end here, her hated moniker, which, gross). The Doctor scans Poppy’s DNA without asking Belinda’s permission first which, again, is a far cry from the defiant and independent woman from the beginning of the season who told him where he could stick it when he did that to her. It should be pretty apparent why a lot of young queer people have quite reasonably reacted with “fuck that” to this narrative. It’s Davies’ prerogative to explore his feelings around not having children and the sublimated desire for that as an older gay man who’s partly by choice partly by circumstance locked out of that world, but it’s equally the prerogative of younger millennial and Gen Z viewers (who are increasingly hostile to the idea of having children at all in this waking nightmare of a world) to react to this with horror as perilously walking the same line as Conrad’s conservative fantasy. And RTD goes and does the exact same thing with Pregnant Anita! The wish dream we end up with is parenthood and the queer are locked out of it. The intent isn’t awful but by god the result is.
        
        I think it’s by a mile the most regressive and misogynistic ending any companion has had in twenty years of new Who. It ends up with us barely knowing Belinda at all as a coherent person beyond “is mother, wants to get home to daughter”. Really, really iffy stuff. Oh the irony that people say Moffat had the issues around women.

    Watched on a little table in a balcony at Atlanta airport, waiting for a connection to visit the US for my father in law’s funeral. An odd context for this episode. In that context, very welcome as a distraction.
    
    Too chaotic and compromised for me to honestly say it was good, too full of wonderful moments to want to call it bad I guess it’s fitting that as the show sails into its Commissioning Shrug, it sort of falls apart altogether.
    
    The good: The Rani. Making her a scientific racist, a Gallifrey first eugenicist? A good, coherent conception of the character. No notes. “Well it’s goodnight from me” created a weird guffaw from me that unsettled the Atlanta-ans, except for the small child that wanted me to admire their toy owl.
    
    The reappearance of Anita and the way the Time Hotel allowed normality to blow through UNIT HQ? A nice bit of through season plotting. A gun you don’t even realise has been placed on the mantle. The sort of thing that should please fans who don’t like RTD’s plotting normally. It treats Doctor Who as a coherent world with rules that continue to be in place from story to story. And the character and actress are so likeable it’s a sheer pleasure to catch up.
    
    Seeing Jodie Whittaker get material she could make something of – without compromising or rewriting the character – is a bit of genius and makes me sad for the era that never really brought her into focus.
    
    I thought Omega was used well – calling him the Titan fits with his role as an exiled, prehistoric giant of Time Lord society and his becoming a rotted corpse sort of mirrors and extends the decay of his character between the Three Doctors and Arc of Infinity.
    
    The bad: I’m afraid the Baby Poppy material sat badly with me. I truly don’t think that plot coheres either mechanically or aesthetically. Poppy is…not Captain Poppy but when the Doctor and Belinda were forced into Conrad’s world, the Doctor’s memory of Poppy, a baby he met once, inspired the creation of Wish Poppy? Who is also a genuine, biological mix of The Doctor and Bel? But not the product of her wishes and memories? And being forced into this relationship saw the Doctor sitting up alone drinking and Belinda running into the woods to scream?
    
    And the happy ending is Belinda’s life is rewritten so she’s a mother – exactly the thing she ran weeping from one episode earlier? And she’s raising baby as a single parent, working as a nurse for the NHS…that’s not the house of someone in that situation. I’m DWM RTD talked about reshooting the opening of the series to turn Belinda’s house into a house share because it didn’t ring true. While you have to ask how it got through multiple drafts and actually in front of cameras without anyone saying “this is not what reality is like”, it’s good they cared to fix it. The reversion at the end to baseless moneyed comfort just contributes to this sense that something unacceptable is being smoothed over.
    
    I just, truly do not get this. I don’t understand it on an intellectual level, I don’t feel it in my guts. There’s no level of symbolism or theme I see it playing to. Poppy is just declared by authorial fiat to be ‘real’, unlike everything else created or changed by Conrad’s wishes. Is there not a world of other wish babies created by forcing everyone into heterosexual hell? Do they not count?
    
    The treatment of Conrad is complex and I admire that attempted complexity. I’m not certain I buy the idea that Ruby would call Conrad’s world nice. It’s a minor detail that sours the scene for me. “You thought this was nice”, “This is what kindness is for you”…there’s other permutations of the line that capture the meaning and carry the scene forward without actually saying Conrad is kind. I think it’s a shame because it biffs the complexity the scene attempts. It’s off by one degree.
    
    The Doctor and Bel’s treatment of Ruby towards the end seemed like an incredibly bum note to me. It’s not like I want the show to have the goodies being explicitly being lovely all the time. But what is meant to be a sinister moment of the Doctor and Belinda behaving ‘like normal’ instead seems to become them behaving uncharacteristically shittily to Ruby. It’s dissonant, but the wrong kind of dissonant.
    
    And then, there’s the ending: on the one hand, it’s incredibly visible that the episode that existed had to be smashed up and turned into a regeneration story. It feels like a crisis. What on earth was going on with Susan and Poppy showing up in the run up? There’s such a chaotic sense that things have gone wrong. And yet it’s done with generosity. Jodie Whittaker, the incredible, rich lighting shining into the darkened TARDIS is a beautiful, artful shot that doesn’t feel like the last minute panic the production was in. “I don’t want to do this alone” and throwing open the door to be with the universe I loved. Joy to the world less so.
    
    And Billie Piper. On one hand, on paper it sounds ludicrous and desperate. On the other it won me over instantly and I want to see more. Such charm and charisma in that moment of performance.
    
    Who knows where we go from here. This was a season where it felt to like the show had its mojo back. It was motoring along, always trying, reaching, finding things to say and having fun. I want to see more but I ache for a bit of consistency.

After puttung his life on hold to care for his dying partner, Russell then poured himself back into writing, and television in particular. I can’t help but read that in relation to what the Doctor was prepared to do: end his life, or lives, trying to fix the vortex itself, which is both life (the Bad Wolf’s resurrection of Jack) and death (the vortex energy killing Nine after removing it from Rose).     I mean. It’s a subjective, personal opinion but there’s nothing so depressing to me as the phrase “Returning Monster”. It’s not particularly about Sutekh or The Rani or Omega or the Master, the Daleks and the Cybermen or (groan) the Midnight Entity. For me it’s about the fanfictification of Doctor Who. Or, if you like, the Big Finish Syndrome. “I was impressed by this monster or villain when I was ten so, now I’ll bring them back but this time I’ll do it right!”
    
    So, of course, while zero knowledge of the Classic Era is necessary to appreciate these episodes and their returning Big Bads, the nagging question, for me, is “why bother if the said Big Bad turns out to be a shaggy dog story?
    
    If all we ask of our Doctor Who is that it shows us something we haven’t seen before what possible value can there be in showing us old timers something we’ve seen before and at the same time showing new viewers something they haven’t seen before but that is referenced as something that has been seen before? If the reason is to tempt new viewers with a suggestion of some deep “lore” it is probably a good idea to make that “lore” at least interesting and ideally a riveting, thought provoking and terrifying experience.
    
    Or why not be creative instead? Why, in an era that can produce ‘73 Yards’, ‘Dot and Bubble’ and ‘The Story and the Engine’, an era in the wider world that can create ‘Black Mirror’ and ‘The Umbrella Academy’ (and I acknowledge YMMV on those shows) do we need to cobble together a bombastic, CGI overloaded Doctor Who finale that turns out to be a damp squib, involving a final battle with said returned adversary resolved either by a deus ex machina, a reset button or just absolute buggery bollocks techno babble.
    
    As to viewing figures. Yes, they are down across the board and I couldn’t care less but clearly any streaming service or content provider is going to be deciding on the continuation of a co-production deal based on the number of views the show got, as well as audience reaction online or elsewhere. Or am I missing something?
    
    Incidentally, the comments on this site were once a treasure trove of incisive theory and intelligent analysis; leavened by subjectivity, personal opinion, foibles and some very idiosyncratic views. I have, in the past derived a great deal of enjoyment from reading the observations and reactions to Dr. Sandifer’s reviews from other lovers of my favourite TV show and responding to them here.
    
    Anyway here’s my subjective opinion.
    
    I would very much like Doctor Who to be gently put to sleep for a while. A second hiatus until such time as some future show-runner with a vision for how the show can fulfil its potential of innovation and surprise can revive it. Let that take as long as it takes but whatever happens can we please not have any more “returning monsters”.
    
    [Reply](https://www.eruditorumpress.com/blog/the-reality-war-review?replytocom=267182#respond)
    
51.  ![Image 207](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/c17efb840d44b5bfb0bba507e6bf67fad1f6501ef1c3b21c9a40ef359376c2ae?s=48&d=mm&r=g) Trevor M  
    July 26, 2025 @ 11:23 am
    
    Having just watched the last 2 episodes of the season, my overriding feeling is that watching this show has become an empty ritual. One that Disney and BBC executives might save me from if I’m unable to save myself.
    
    There have been times where the Gatwa/Davies run has been a bit of an improvement from the complete emptiness of Flux, but the Reality War has in some ways brought me back to that same sensation of emptiness. Barely anything in this show feels like it has consequence. Of course no fictional show really has consequence, but good ones feel like they matter. Whereas Doctor Who tries to persuade me that Poppy is worth changing the universe for, and worth the nearest thing the Doctor has to suicide, and the show completely failed to do anything to make me care about Poppy’s existence or lack thereof.
    
    Watching the show is an exercise in time management. I don’t really watch anything as it comes out, that’s just me nowadays, but Doctor Who did used to be something I would try to get to quickly. Now, I’m not even that keen about avoiding spoilers. I think mostly I watch it just so that I can say I’ve watched every episode, or watched a reconstruction with the original audio for all those ones in the 1960s we no longer have. I’m a completist. Gotta watch ’em all.
    
    There definitely are episodes I still get something out of. And this did have its moments, such as Archie Panjabi in UNIT HQ. But too often the big flashy episodes give me the experience of hoping for moments that land. And hoping. And hoping. And losing hope.

_“The concept of time-travel, paradox and alternate reality has always been mind-blowing and now a mind-blowing novel to live up to it.  Hollywood check this out!”_ — [Bookish Things](http://lesleymc.blogspot.co.uk/2012/03/reality-war-slough-of-despond.html) 5 stars

_“Terse, tense and emotional, the_ _Slough of Despond_ _generates a cool balance between science, history and human relationship.”_ —[The Green Porch](http://davidmarkbrownwrites.com/rrs-roundup-lizard-brains-and-terminal-viscosity/)

In 1992, Radlan Saravanan runs a small business out of a Tudor cottage in the sleepy English village of Elstow. But Radlan was born in 2951, and when he falls in love with a local girl, he has to choose between running from his own people and condemning his lover to die.

He makes _the wrong choice_.

Travelling into the past, falling in love… it turns out that he was _meant_ to do these things. He’s been manipulated all along. But now he’s slipped his handlers, and Time isn’t following the right script any more. Other versions of history vie for dominance, and our human reality is losing.

In 1992, Radlan Saravanan sparked _The Reality War._

[![Image 3](https://timctaylor.files.wordpress.com/2012/01/reality-war2.jpg?w=225&h=300)](http://timctaylor.files.wordpress.com/2012/01/reality-war2.jpg)

_The Reality War_ is a two-novel series loosely inspired by _The Pilgrim’s Progress_, and set in Bedfordshire. It is both an action-adventure series, and a spiritual journey made by two people, mirror images of each other from rival realities.

_The Reality War Book1: The Slough of Despond_ is available now as a Kindle and ePUB eBook, and in paperback.

_The Reality War Book2: The City of Destruction_ is out now for Kindle and ePUB. Paperback edition to follow – expected end of September 2012.
